These days it's firmly upscale — prices have crept up. If you're still imagining this as a casual neighborhood cocktail spot, it's time to recalibrate those expectations.

The first thing that strikes you is the room itself. Those famous Ludwig Bemelmans murals still wrap around the walls in their whimsical glory, depicting Central Park scenes with rabbits ice skating and characters that could have wandered out of the Madeline books. The dim lighting, live piano music, and Art Deco touches create an atmosphere that genuinely transports you to another era. On my visit, the pianist was working through a sophisticated jazz repertoire that perfectly matched the room's energy without overwhelming conversation.

But let's talk about what you'll actually pay for this experience. Cocktails now hover around $30-35, and that's before tip. I ordered their signature Bemelmans Martini — beautifully executed, perfectly cold, generous pour — but it came with a $32 price tag. My companion's Old Fashioned was equally well-crafted and similarly priced. Some older posts I'd read suggested this was a splurge but still accessible spot; that's no longer quite accurate. You're looking at $70-80 minimum for two drinks per person if you stay for a couple of rounds.

The crowd reflected this pricing. On a Thursday around 8 PM, I saw well-dressed couples celebrating anniversaries, what appeared to be successful business dealings being toasted, and a few tourists who'd clearly saved up for the experience. Service was impeccable — attentive without being intrusive, knowledgeable about the menu, and genuinely warm. Our server guided us through their seasonal cocktails with real enthusiasm and made excellent recommendations based on our preferences.

The bar snacks have also evolved. We ordered the mixed nuts ($18) and smoked almonds ($16), which would have seemed outrageous a few years ago but felt consistent with the current positioning. They were exceptional quality, but still — $16 almonds.

Is it worth it? That depends entirely on what you're after. For a special occasion or to experience a genuine piece of New York history in an environment that's maintained its standards, absolutely. The combination of those murals, live music, expert bartending, and old-world atmosphere is increasingly rare. Back then Williamsburg was still mostly empty warehouses and art studios, and walking into that place felt like stepping into a different century — which I suppose it was, since the building's been there since 1887. Every time I go back, and I probably go three or four times a year, the feeling doesn't change.

The dark wood interior, those Tiffany-style lamps, the way the waiters call you "Chief" or "Sweetheart" regardless of who you are — it's a time capsule. The room is smaller and more intimate than people expect. Those deep wooden booths, the pressed-tin ceiling, the whole place has this warm, amber glow that just wraps around you. It's cosy in a way no modern steakhouse manages to pull off.

The entrance has a couple of steps up, which always makes me think — it's not the easiest place to get into if you've got mobility issues, and I don't recall ever seeing a ramp. It's a very old building and that's just how it is, but it's something to be aware of.

I usually drive in from Park Slope and I've gotten good at finding parking on Rutledge or Roebling Street after 6 PM when the restaurant traffic dies down. There's a lot nearby too if you don't want to circle.

The bacon — God, the bacon. That thick slab of sweet-smoked pork belly hasn't changed in two decades. Same recipe, same sizzle. My order hasn't changed either: bacon for the table, porterhouse for two medium-rare (for me and whoever I'm dragging along), creamed spinach, German potatoes. The steak comes out on that pewter platter still hissing, and the waiters slice it tableside with this quiet ceremony that feels almost religious.

Is it the same as it was twenty years ago? Pretty much. The prices have climbed — that porterhouse was maybe $70 back then — but the quality hasn't slipped. The staff turnover seems minimal. I saw the same maître d' last month that I remember from my first visit. He's probably been there forty years.

For me, that's the draw. It's not just dinner — it's a connection to a version of New York that's mostly disappeared. Places like this don't open anymore.
